html:
On the spring festival of Vaisakhi in 1699, at Anandpur in the Punjab hills, Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa, the order of initiated Sikhs.

The story is told this way. Before a great crowd he asked who would give his head for the faith. Five men stepped forward, one at a time, from different castes and regions. They became the Panj Pyare, the five beloved. He initiated them with sweetened water stirred with a sword, and then asked them to initiate him.

Members of the Khalsa:

  • Keep the five Ks, among them uncut hair and a steel bracelet.
  • Take the name Singh, lion, for men and Kaur, princess, for women, setting aside caste names.
  • Are sworn to defend the faith and the weak.

The Guru's father, Guru Tegh Bahadur, had been executed under Aurangzeb in 1675, and the Sikhs faced Mughal and hill rajas' armies. The Khalsa made Sikhism a disciplined community able to fight. A century later its warriors formed the Sikh Empire of Ranjit Singh.
sum: On the spring festival of Vaisakhi in 1699, at Anandpur in the Punjab hills, Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa, the order of initiated Sikhs.
